#4793. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4791. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4790. What Does It Mean to Believe in God?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

In his Ethics, Aristotle says that we should seek to understand each thing according to the kind of account it permits. In solving an arithmetic problem, for example, we should expect an answer that is both accurate and precise. In the moral life, by contrast, we should seek an account that accords with what a practically wise person would have to say.

If we are adding or subtracting single-digit numbers, we can reasonably expect a reliable answer from a third grader. If, however, we are talking about friendship, marriage, or the relationship between a parent and offspring, we should turn elsewhere for insight, perhaps to the works of George Eliot or Leo Tolstoy.

A similar shift in expectation is appropriate when we think about belief in God. If God were a phenomenon susceptible to the sort of reasoning that we find in an arithmetic problem or a proof in symbolic logic, then it should be relatively easy to construct a knock-down argument for the existence and nature of God.

If, however, God is not quantifiable, then arithmetical approaches are not likely to serve us well, and if God is not like the major or minor premises of a syllogism (such as: All things we can conceive of exist; we can conceive of God; therefore, God exists), then we should not expect to “solve” God like a proof.

Likewise, if God is not made of matter, we should not expect to be able to reproduce the divine presence through scientific means, whether physical or chemical. The mere fact that God does not have mass, dimension, shape, location, or color does not establish that God is nothing more than a figment of human imagination.

After all, we believe in numbers, although they lack all the physical properties just mentioned, and we also believe in love, justice, beauty, and truth, although they too cannot be counted, logically proved, or reproduced in a laboratory flask. There are things we believe to be real that we cannot see with our eyes or touch with our hands.

If sacred texts are any guide, the best means we have of accounting for God are not the methods of mathematics, logic, or science, but those more closely aligned with literature or narrative. The Bible, for example, is full of stories, and while a few of these stories include God directly, many more address the effects of God’s presence in the unfolding of the human story.

In one well-known metaphor, God is not something we directly apprehend, but we can sense God at work in the world much as we see and hear the breeze rustling the leaves on a tree. When Moses first senses God’s presence, it is in the form of a bush that is burning but not consumed by the flames, something only he has the curiosity and patience to see.

At this point, a skeptic might ask, If God is real, is it too much to ask that the divine should simply appear before us, work a few miracles, and thereby remove all doubt? But what if the problem is not God’s but ours? What if God cannot be put into any humanly constructed box because the divine is far beyond our meager intellectual and imaginative capacities?

What if we are talking about a reality that undergirds all of reality, not only as we know it but also far beyond our capacity to comprehend? What if we are seeking not just a clockmaker who set things in motion billions of years ago but a creator who sustains the universe from moment to moment as it continues to unfold even now in space and time?

Even the physical universe is far beyond our capacity to keep tabs on. A mature human organism consists of about 40 trillion cells, each one of which performs about 1 billion chemical reactions per second, which in turn requires the presence of about 100 trillion atoms of hydrogen. Of course, these are just round numbers – only God knows for sure.

It is quite possible, perhaps likely, and based on past experience, all but certain that there is a great deal that we do not yet know about even the physical universe. It was only in 1895 that we first learned of the existence of x-rays and only in 1962 that we verified extra-terrestrial x-ray sources. What else still awaits our discovery?

Yet even to say that we still have a great deal more to discover hardly captures the full extent of the problem. For one thing, there may be more out there and in here, even if it is susceptible to our awareness or understanding, than we will ever uncover. And it is also possible that the greater part of it does not conform to our ways of knowing.

Perhaps being itself, as well as its source and end, is not an entirely anthropomorphic thing, in the sense that it is not built for our minds. It may have many other purposes far beyond us. And yet, here we are, blessed with the ability to perceive and understand some truly remarkable things, even if we can’t begin to get our hands around the whole thing.

Perhaps when it comes to God, poetry, music, art, and narrative are the best we can hope for – intimations, always allusive and never definitive. And yet, even here, we find truth and beauty for which we have every reason to be deeply thankful, for perhaps it is above all when we sense God’s presence, maybe with the aid of Eliot and Tolstoy, that we come most fully to life.

#4789. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4788. Two Novel Solutions If You're Stuck in a Loneliness Trap

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Though we understand that nostalgia is a powerful state—a sentimental longing for the past— we may fall short of harnessing it to transform our lives. A 2014 study published in Self and Identity found that experiencing nostalgia not only evokes positive emotions but also fosters personal growth. This growth is largely driven by positive self-regard, a key psychological resource, one that bolsters nostalgia.

Interestingly, the study also found that nostalgia strengthened feelings of belonging and provided a sense of meaning. These elements help counter loneliness. Here are two tips to make the most of your nostalgic reveries to counter feelings of loneliness and disconnection.

A prescient quote from the hit show The Office goes: “I wish there were a way to know you’re in ‘the good old days’ before you’ve actually left them.”

The crucial insight is that people often don't recognize the value of experiences while living through them, but tend to view them more positively in retrospect. And this isn’t just anecdotal.

A classic study published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology explored how people anticipate, experience, and remember significant life events. Participants were divided into groups, each assigned to different events like vacations or trips. They were asked to anticipate these events, record their actual experiences during them, and then recall these experiences after some time had passed.

The study found that when participants recalled these events later, their memories were predominantly positive, more so than the actual experience. Negative aspects seemed to fade, leaving a “rosier” memory.

Once you embrace that you will long for your past, no matter how lonely it may seem now, you are more likely to create joyful experiences and memories. This can mean striking up a conversation with your barista, joining a volunteer group, or even a stroll in a park—you never know who you may run into.

Rosy retrospection empowers us to invest more in our daily interactions, not necessarily with grand expectations, but with an appreciation for their future value in our memories. The trick is recognizing the potential in ordinary moments to become extraordinary, nostalgic memories.

A recent study published in Emotion shows how nostalgia can benefit individuals grappling with loneliness. The study found that for those who often feel a lack of direction or meaning in life—a common issue among the lonely—engaging in nostalgia can have a significant positive effect.

This may be about recalibrating your sense of self in relation to the people around you. Think of it this way: Lonely individuals often feel like side characters in their own lives, often being overwhelmed by their isolation. Experiencing nostalgia (either spontaneous or self-induced) can help recenter their narrative, provided they contextualize the emotions and memories that are associated with the experience.

If you’d like to contextualize and make the most of your nostalgia to regain a sense of meaning in your life, you can try the Hero’s Journey method. This approach involves effective storytelling, where you take charge of your life’s narrative through seven key steps:

By mindfully engaging with nostalgia, you can weave a narrative that highlights your journey, underlines your growth, and reinforces your place within a larger community. This approach can combat loneliness and finding meaning.

Our memories are not just a source of comfort but also a bridge to a more fulfilling present. Nostalgia can be a powerful ally in easing loneliness, especially if you can look beyond the passive experience of it. Reflecting on positive past experiences can reframe how you view your current life situation. Generally, we remember the past as rosier than it was, which can help us appreciate the people in our lives more and foster better connections.

However, tummy control typically comes with a bit more compression, which may not be great for lower-impact activities like yoga or casual walks.

Again, length is up to your personal preference, but the most flattering cut is typically just above your ankle. For most people, that means a 7/8 style of leggings. Full-length leggings, or ones that extend all the way to your feet, might be better for barefoot workouts like yoga. Other lengths, like capri leggings, are really up to your personal style.

#4786. The Joy of Reading

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

As a college professor for over 30 years, I have worked with countless students who either claim they hate reading or report that they've never finished an entire book. To succeed in college, it’s important to read what’s assigned. It’s also important to read for pleasure. Why? Because, simply put, it makes you more interesting.

With students nearing the end of the semester and hopefully thinking about how they can improve their habits and skills for the new semester, it is worth thinking about the role of reading. With the holiday break almost upon us, it's the perfect time to practice and to embark on a potentially interesting book.

People who read have a greater sense of fluency of ideas and perspectives that they can bring to bear on conversations, and they possess stronger vocabularies. These qualities give people an edge both socially and professionally. Referencing something you read and learned that resonates with you or naturally relates to a conversation during a job interview, for example, helps position you as someone with insight and depth.

The other thing to remember is that the habit of reading often translates to greater agility with writing. When you have more exposure to a variety of ways that ideas are expressed, you’re able to gather more information to craft what you want to say.

College is a great time to discover exactly what it is that you like to read. This is especially true if you’re coming to college with little interest in reading. This lack of interest is often due to not having had much say in what you got to read in high school. So, now’s the time to think about what you gravitate to most. What do you find most moving and compelling? Maybe it’s fiction, nonfiction, creative nonfiction, or poetry. Whatever it is, reading is a passport for the experience of world-traveling, which is a gift you can give yourself.

If your parents read to you when you were a child, they may have shown you the value and joy of reading. I’ve started directly asking my students if a parent or guardian read to or with them, what their favorite book was as a child, and what their favorite is now. What’s most sad for me is when students aren’t able to name a single book and instead tell me they “never read,” “never had a parent read to me,” “hate reading,” or “never finished a book.”

But even if the value of reading was not instilled in you growing up, it’s not too late to develop a habit of reading for pleasure. Find something that potentially interests you, put your phone away where it’s not even visible, grab a fun drink or snack, and curl up in a cozy space and read. Try just 15 minutes at first. If you like it, keep going. If you find yourself restless or sleepy, try to push through a bit longer, and if that doesn’t work then go do something else and make a commitment to yourself to return to the book the next day. Typically, those in the regular practice of reading and enjoying it generally find it easier to be alone and enjoy solitude.

In summary, when college students work to strengthen their reading muscle, both in terms of reading for classes and for pleasure, they encounter the following benefits:

#4785. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4783. Later Daters Still Love Sex

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Among many destructive, ageist stereotypes prevalent in America, one of the most pervasive is that older adults aren’t interested in, capable of, or engaged in having sex. On the contrary, research shows that about three-quarters of those aged 57-64, over half of those aged 65-74, and a quarter of those aged 75-85 had sexual contact with someone in the past year. And this doesn’t even count those who would have chosen to have sex but had no opportunity.

While the stereotypes are alive and well regarding the nability of older adults to have sex, many, if not most, either do have, or are interested in having, sexual activity with a partner. It’s true older adults may struggle with aspects of sex they didn’t confront when younger—men with the ability to maintain erections or ejaculate; women with lubrication or discomfort. But there are excellent treatments for these conditions, and humans are creative. Older adults engage in satisfying romantic relationships without sexual activity, satisfying sexual relationships without romance, and everything in between. And in terms of sex, older couples not only enjoy intercourse, but also non-penetrative sexual activities like hugging, cuddling, sleeping naked; manual, masturbatory, and oral play activities, and more.

A recent study by Harris and Melanson (2026) interviewed 100 single older adults aged 60-83 (50 women and 50 men) recruited from dating sites for gender, racial, and educational diversity. More older adults are single today than ever before (due to longer lives and the acceptance of divorce), and this group is understudied compared to older adults with partners. The Harris and Melanson study was limited by heterosexual participants, but we can extrapolate many of its findings to all relationships:

Sex is a healthy part of life throughout adulthood, whether one is single, partnered, or in between. How it looks and when it happens may change, and some adults may do well without a partner, but the majority of older adults, like younger adults, find partnered sex an important ingredient of healthy social lives, life satisfaction, and wellbeing.

Harris and Melanson surveyed an often-ignored group of older adults—those who are single. Because they found them through dating sites, we know participants in the sample were at least somewhat interested in pursuing romantic and/or sexual partnerships. It’s up to future researchers to explore whether single older adults not interested in dating are equally interested in sex (with another person), or simply feel content alone; as well as how these results may be different in LGBTQ+ and other marginalized populations.

Harris, L., & Melanson, C. (2026). “The Shop Is Not Closed”: Sex and Sexuality Among Older Adult Daters. The Journal of Sex Research, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1080/00224499.2026.2614315

#4782. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4781. Inside the World of an Intimacy Coordinator

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Recently, after seeing a stage play, I spoke to a lead actor about how she is able to feel safe during physically intimate scenes in front of an audience. She told me that there is an intimacy coordinator who comes onto the set to make sure the actors’ feelings about intimacy with other actors are taken into account. She has also worked on film sets with an intimacy coordinator when she felt uneasy and vulnerable in front of the camera and crew and her lover in the film.

I wanted to find out more about this and, unexpectedly, I met intimacy coordinator Christina McHugh at an event in New Mexico a few weeks later. I asked her to define what it is that she does when she is hired to work on films. “Old-fashioned doctors went house to house, a mail person goes door to door, and an intimacy coordinator goes set to set.” The geographical areas she covered were Albuquerque, Santa Fe, and movie ranches. She goes from one set to another.

She explained that making actors feel psychologically and physically safe was mostly prep work, before the scenes were shot. She had extensive conversations with directors and then worked with the actors to find out what their boundaries were and to get their consent. “Then I would go back to the director and impart information like the fact that the actor wanted less nudity. I would ask the director if it could be filmed a different way.”

For filming sex scenes, she used things like a “half-deflated Pilates ball to put between the actors’ crotches. There were often three layers of barriers between the actors for simulated sex. If the woman is on top of the man, her bouncing is done with a 9-inch Pilates ball that makes it look like simulated sex.”

McHugh said that her job entails negotiating boundaries with individual actors, the director, and trying to get all sides to agree. This is especially true in building trust on the set of a film with hyper-exposure, that includes nudity, simulated sex, and sexual violence.

Some of the sets she worked on include "Better Call Saul," "Pluribus," "Love Lies Bleeding," "Obliterated," "Duster," "The Cleaning Lady," "Waco," and "Dead for a Dollar."

I inquired where she learned her profession, and she replied that she trained with the Intimacy Professionals Association. “In about 2017, it was the first time it showed up in a credit line. It started with an HBO series, "The Deuce," which was about the porn industry. The actress felt she was being treated as a porn star and not an actress.”

I believed her when McHugh said you need a spine made of titanium to deal with producers and directors. She is not flippant about the issues actors have when she is negotiating with them. She said that young female actors tell her about being victims of sexual predation, and she takes care of them. This is an important part of her job, which she takes very seriously.

Entertainment writer Liz Konkel had this to say in a recent post on Cinema Blend: “The rules have certainly changed in regard to how sex scenes are filmed, thanks to the rise of intimacy coordinators on sets. Now, this doesn't mean we don't get plenty of steamy content. However, what it does mean is that more technical work goes into creating such scenes. In a post #MeToo Movement industry, these coordinators also help ensure actors feel comfortable and protected during intimate scenes.”

In the same article, she also addressed how actors’ boundaries and trust concerns were dealt with before intimacy coordinators. “Back in the early aughts, scenes were seemingly required of the actors if it was in the script. However, some performers have since shared stories where trust was taken advantage of on set. For instance, "Basic Instinct’s" Sharon Stone has made claims involving inappropriate requests for nudity amid production. With that, many now consider intimacy coordinators to be essential.”

#4780. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4779. Making Change Happen

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

So, you realize that the way you have been going about things doesn’t work. You might not like the way you behave or your experience of relationships. You might not like the way you feel or how your emotions impact your decisions. And you know that if you don’t turn things around, you are going to keep repeating the same cycle. But people often struggle to change even when they genuinely want to.

I cringe when I hear people say “That’s just the way I am” while at the same time complaining about the state of their relationships. Some people use that statement to avoid responsibility. They believe their personality characteristics are fixed or have repeatedly failed in their efforts to foster change within themselves. So, rather than putting effort into changing themselves, many people prefer that others would simply come to their senses and accommodate them.

You can always work on changing the environment, and this is usually what people try first. They try to convince, persuade, nudge, and manipulate others… or they shut themselves off interpersonally, go into denial, or resort to blame and attack. But these efforts rarely result in lasting positive outcomes, and people stay happy only as long as the environment is cooperating.

Here is my recommended outline for lasting change and understanding why change can be so hard. I recommend taking these steps sequentially, as they build on each other in a cumulative fashion.

If you want to change yourself, you first need to consider what “self” you are referring to. Changing your entire being may seem insurmountable and lead you to give up before you even start. But many psychological theorists view the self as multifaceted. In other words, we are all groupings of associated parts, and we can use our more developed parts to help shape and coach the less developed ones that we are trying to change.

Sometimes change means de-emphasizing one previously dominant part of your personality and strengthening a part that was previously dormant.

People are often ambivalent about change and might actually get something out of maintaining their negative behaviors.

Before you lay aside your own ambivalence, let’s see what you actually get out of the behavior or experience you say you want to let go of. What will you lose if you change? What are the factors arguing against it?

Become conscious of your own resistance. Before evoking your commitment to a new course of action, it might help to first write down all of the positive things you get out of it. For example, what if you want to cut down on your drinking? Drinking might help you gain social acceptance and feel less lonely. It might help you relax and escape your anxiety and internal demons. Or it might simply help you escape boredom and give you something to do. These are all reasonable goals, and before you lay down the booze, you might want to consider how you are going to meet them.

But then you must ask yourself, what would need to change first before the behavior can change? Problematic behaviors are often not consciously chosen but, rather, come about through how we regulate our emotions— for example, putting too much pressure on an ambivalent romantic partner, talking too much about your insecurities, or getting aggravated and shutting down when interactions with a relationship partner get touchy.

In these examples, the root cause is often difficulty controlling your emotions.

Sometimes, your rational brain knows what it wants to do, but your emotional brain just won’t cooperate.

You should learn about how people with your personality style regulate anxiety. For example, a person with an avoidant attachment style will most likely regulate anxiety by withdrawing, shutting down, or dominating. A person with an anxious attachment style is most likely to regulate emotions by pressing too hard for reassurance or oversharing.

Learn about your personality and attachment style… then you will have an easier time changing your behavior. In other words, your conscious brain will understand what your emotional brain is doing and how to keep it from taking over.

Sometimes you just need an attitude adjustment. In the preceding paragraphs, I outlined how subconscious processes, like regulating emotions, influence behavior. But sometimes, behavior comes from the more conscious parts of your mind. In other words, your emotions follow your thoughts instead of the other way around. Attitudes are consciously held statements that you tell yourself about the way things are. You can change your attitudes by watching your self-talk and what you say to yourself in your head. Don’t expect to have angry, intolerant thoughts and be able to pull off controlling your emotions and acting loving.

If you want to change a part of yourself, it often helps to have another part supervise the process and give you supportive feedback. Take the example of inner child work. I’ve spoken about this previously in my posts. Although I’m not specifically recommending it here, it serves as a case in point.

In this approach, you learn to view your less mature, emotional, or wounded aspects of self as the child you once were. Often, that child will have gone through some difficult times that forced him/her to learn to regulate emotions and view the world in ways that don’t serve you well in adulthood. To heal this part of ourselves, we practice seeing it as a separate entity (child). The rational/adult part of our brain then gets to serve as the caring and supportive adult caregiver who can contain and advise the more emotional and less controlled part.

Sometimes when you make positive changes, the immediate result might seem negative. For example, if you quit drinking, all of your drinking buddies might get uncomfortable hanging out with you. In short, you might lose access to your old social support system and access to romantic partners if you are single. Addressing the social support issue is one of the main reasons people consider 12-step meetings. In this case, even though the short-term impact of not drinking could seem negative, the long-term impact is likely to be healthier friends and a more sustainable, healthy lifestyle.

Similarly, if you change some of your behaviors within your family system, like caretaking others, controlling, or being in the problem or “sick role,” the short-term outcome might not feel positive. Families (and work/friend systems) usually are in some sort of emotional balance (called homeostasis). When one person changes their role in the system, it throws the system out of balance, and everyone else has to adjust their behaviors or roles to accommodate the change. Some people in the system might not like the change or the disequilibrium it creates, and they may act out in an attempt to pull you back into your role. So, the short-term impact might be to feel more cut off or alienated from family members, but the long-term impact might be healthier long-term relationships that work for you.

To summarize: The suggestions I put forward in this post just touch the surface of what really would encompass a book. But I believe these are some of the most actionable principles available to get you started. And, above all, be sure to give yourself some grace and self-compassion… and this alone will do wonders to help you make change happen.

McConnell, A. R. (2011). The multiple self-aspects framework: Self-concept representation and its implications. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 15(1), 3–27.

#4777. Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.
