#4776. The Psychology of Miracles

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The human psyche has always upheld a tireless faith in the extraordinary. When tragic events decimate our sense of safety and security, such as an unexpected medical diagnosis, a devastating personal crisis, or a profound loss, we seldom default to reason. Instead, we survey horizons looking for signs and wishing for the seemingly impossible to step in and rescue us from the inevitable.

This reaction is not rare. Surveys from Gallup and Pew Research show that up to 79 percent of U.S. adults believe in miracles, while more than 67 percent strongly believe in phenomena beyond scientific explanation. When reason falls arguably short, divine intervention becomes the next best thing.

For millennia, our existence has relied heavily on our ancestors’ ability to anticipate threats and secure their surroundings. This important skill helped to avoid near-certain death from starvation or the elements, in the event we were ostracized from our tribe. The robust urge to create some kind of order in a confusing and hostile world was paramount. Consequently, strict cause-and-effect accounts often fall emotionally flat. Whenever we are confronted with catastrophic hardship or existential dread, statistics might explain how an event occurred, but oftentimes it can't answer more profound human questions.

Whenever human beings reframe a striking coincidence as divine intervention or maybe even the hand of God, you have to wonder: Is it simply impulsive denial, or is it a hardwired inclination to believe in the supernatural? Accordingly, it's hard to negate the obvious that perhaps miracles act as psychological defense mechanisms—safeguards explicitly designed to protect us from crippling despair. That's why we so often hear overused proverbs like “Everything happens for a reason” and “God works in mysterious ways.”

Whenever we utilize this defense mechanism, the human mind reclaims a sense of agency when circumstances beyond our control leave us feeling powerless. Anticipating miracles helps to regulate the body's built-in stress response by lowering cortisol levels (the stress hormone) and sustaining emotional stamina during prolonged crisis. It's part of our evolutionary adaptation—a sophisticated cognitive mechanism intended to stimulate hope, develop resilience, and drive us forward even when the odds are stacked against us. Novelist and philosopher Fyodor Dostoevsky, who profoundly examined human psychology, wrote, “since man cannot live without miracles, he will provide himself with miracles of his own making."

But like most things in life, there are downsides to having a miracle mindset. Shielding us from hopelessness and relying too heavily on the mystical can pose psychological, medical, and existential risks. For instance, individuals might reject evidence-based medical treatments, therapeutic interventions, and, perhaps, lifesaving procedures by instead waiting for an unlikely intervention from above.

Additionally, it can lead to passivity and hesitation when needing to assert free will in making important decisions. It could also cause spiritual injury because when anticipated miracles fail to happen, the ensuing fallout can be debilitating. In place of organically processing grief, people might also assume cosmic guilt, blaming themselves or believing their faith was not strong enough. This could potentially worsen their trauma.

The miracle mindset could also foster detachment from reality, ignoring hard facts, leaving individuals vulnerable to exploitation by predatory people, control groups, and buying into false promises. In the end, it could train the mind to overlook sound rationality and established scientific data that is invaluable to our health and well-being.

In America, presenting cold, hard facts to people who are deeply entrenched in their beliefs can trigger a reaction. For many, perhaps it feels too much like an existential threat, frequently promoting defensiveness and condemnation. Whenever we challenge any kind of sacred doctrine, we invite accusations of blasphemy or a lack of a moral compass.

Our personal beliefs are much more than just opinions. They are vital pillars of safety, identity, and communal belonging. Science demonstrates that when an overpoweringly held worldview is questioned, the brain processes it like a threat of physical danger. It does not compute it as a rational debate, but as a menace to psychological existence.

Finally, believing in miracles fulfills a human need that offers structure and comfort. It helps us manage the fear of what lies beyond more easily. The idea of a meaningless, dark oblivion that lacks determination is hard for many people to swallow. Hence, the concept of divine intervention acts as a soothing balm against uncertainty, providing reassurance in a shaky and unpredictable world.

In addition, every human being feels the omnipresent specter of death. The anxiety around mortality will always be something we have in common. But what separates us is the degree to which we allow fear to govern our choices and our worldviews and how it might compromise our ability to exercise our own free will.

Therefore, how we respond to it is wholly a choice. Perhaps the true measure of our freedom is not how we escape our fear of mortality, but how we live it every day, in spite of it. And sometimes, enduring that reality requires a trace of the supernatural. There’s no harm in a spark of magic in the midst of inescapable tragedy.

As the saying goes (often credited to Albert Einstein), "There are only two ways to live your life: One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.”

#4775. TikTok’s Viral Winter Arc Challenge Is the Best Way to Get a Jump-Start on Your New Year’s Goals

Here's how to make the most of these last few months of the year.

Between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year. While, yes, you should cut yourself some slack here and there during the busy holiday season, it’s also more important now than ever to finish the year strong.

That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play. This annual challenge, which originally went viral on TikTok back in 2024, starts October 1 and ends January 1 (but if you missed the start, it’s not too late!). The only premise: Stay locked in on your goals for the rest of the calendar year, whether that’s training for a half-marathon, hitting your Goodreads book quota, or mastering a new hobby.

This time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, says Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in New York City. Now’s the time for you to “be intentional about your energy and what serves you.”

If you haven’t started the challenge yet, it’s not too late. Whether you try it for 83 or 30 days, the Winter Arc Challenge will set you up for greater success with your New Year’s goals because it’ll strengthen your self-efficacy, or “your sense of belief in your own ability to do what you say that you are going to do,” says Carmichael. Self-efficacy is strengthened through your own behavioral track record, so if you start meeting goals now, you’ll already have momentum heading into January, she explains.

Ready to tackle your own Winter Arc Challenge? Here are some helpful tips to help you make the most of the next few months:

Maybe as part of your Winter Arc Challenge, you aim to cut your monthly spending in half. But a few weeks after setting this goal, you really go overboard at brunches and parties. Don't sweat it. This is “a completely normal part of the change process,” Carmichael says. Instead of giving up when you encounter a relapse here or there, plan for bumps to happen, then get back on track.

So, if you spend too much money one week, instead of falling into a pattern of negative self-talk, replace your thoughts. Carmichael says to plan a script of what you can say to yourself when you relapse, like: “I can still get back on track and feel good about my goals. This is my moment to restart.”

Say you’re planning to work out four times a week until the end of the year. If you know the cold morning weather is going to persuade you to stay under the covers and sleep in, be proactive: Book workout classes online every week so you know they’re in your calendar, and you’re more likely to show up. Also, write down your challenges—like the dropping temps preventing you from leaving your house—to keep yourself accountable, Carmichael adds.

Picture yourself on January 1 having been successful with your Winter Arc Challenge, then move backward and think about everything that led up to it. If your big goal was to do a yoga class every week, visualize yourself walking through the snow to get to your Monday night class, or doing a virtual class at home when there was a bad blizzard. Also think about when you almost skipped classes and fell off the wagon, but you used thought replacements to continue reinforcing your goals. Using imagery will help you mentally prepare for the journey ahead, Carmichael says.

Ask around to see if any of your friends are also doing the Winter Arc Challenge—or if they’re willing to hold you accountable. Then, plan regular meetups or calls to check in. “Talk about how things went with a promise to be honest and supportive if one or both of you is falling off,” Carmichael says. “It will help you to stay consistent when you can leverage your social support network.”

No matter when you started the Winter Arc Challenge, you’ll see and feel the benefits of bettering yourself in no time. Good luck—you got this!

Addison Aloian is the associate health & fitness editor at Women’s Health, where she writes and edits across the health, weight loss, and fitness verticals. #4774. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4773. Why the Clever Hans Analogy Fails Nonspeaking Spellers

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Every time nonspeaking people with autism who spell to communicate make the news, someone brings up Clever Hans. You may know the story: In early 1900s Berlin, a horse seemed to do math, tapping out answers with his hoof. In 1907, the psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed what was really going on. When the questioner knew the answer and Hans could see them, Hans was right about 89% of the time; when the questioner didn't know, or Hans wore blinders, he dropped to about 6%. Questioners unknowingly leaned forward while he tapped and relaxed when he reached the right number, and Hans had learned to stop there.

The suggestion is that spellers are doing the same thing: that the words really come from the person holding the letterboard, either through subtle cues or through the communication partner's unconscious movements (the ideomotor effect). In this post, I draw on my own data and on a year of observations of nonspeaking autistic people to show why this analogy doesn't hold, and why it should be dropped for good. This is not only my personal opinion that comparing nonspeaking autistic people to a horse is cruel; it is also what the facts show.

Hans's trick worked because his task was simple: all he needed was a signal telling him when to stop tapping. Spelling is a different kind of task. To spell a sentence, a person has to choose the right letter out of 26, in the right order, again and again. A single "stop" cue, the kind that worked for Hans, can't do that. Add to this complex dance the sentences that contain words the communication partner doesn't know or normally use, or information nobody in the room expected to hear.

The best evidence here comes from studies that measured how spellers actually spell. In 2020, Vikram Jaswal and his colleagues fitted nine nonspeaking autistic letterboard users with head-mounted eye-trackers while they answered questions about an article read aloud to them, with an assistant holding the board.¹ They pointed to about one letter per second, and 94% of the letters they pointed to were correct. On average, they looked at 71% of the correct letters before pointing to them, about half a second ahead. Like fluent non-autistic typists, they paused longer before the first letter of a new word and were faster on common letter pairs. As the authors point out, cueing would require a separate signal for every letter, picked from 26 options, which would be slow and error-prone. What they found was fast, accurate, and planned.

Some critics argue that the partner moves the board slightly toward the right letter. A 2024 study from the same lab removed the partner entirely.² Thirty-one nonspeaking autistic teenagers and adults played a game on an iPad mounted on a stand, tapping letters as they lit up. No one held the iPad. As a group, they tapped faster when the letters spelled a sentence they had just heard than when similar letters or symbols came in a meaningless order. They were also faster on common letter pairs, and they paused before the first letter of each new word. These are signs of knowing how to spell.

A third study had participants spell on a virtual letterboard in an augmented-reality headset, with no one holding it; they averaged 95.8% accuracy on dictated words.³

If spellers were reading their partners the way Hans read his questioners, blocking their view of the partner should stop them, just as the blinders stopped Hans. As it happens, we've been testing this with a few spellers by placing a rigid panel, about five feet tall and three feet wide, between the speller and the communication partner, so that the spellers cannot see the partners' faces or bodies. The results? They keep spelling fluently and without hesitation. After the very first word, one of them even spelled: "Better with the barrier."

The second problem with the horse analogy is the content. Hans only ever answered questions, and only with answers the questioner already had in mind. Spellers start conversations, ask for things, and say things that surprise the people around them.

A young man I visited this year began spelling at fifteen and spells mainly with his mother. After I spent a full day visiting him at school, he was able that evening to have a conversation about his day and to spell the names of two kids who had visited the classroom; neither his mother nor I knew their names, and his mother hadn't been at school. He was also able to express his feelings towards his brothers and his wish for more independence: "I'm seventeen, let me go by myself," he spelled when he asked to walk to the bus stop alone. Among his other wishes, he asked to go into the ocean with his brothers, wearing a life jacket, and told his parents he wanted a North Face backpack, not the Under Armour one they had picked.

When his mother first began spelling with him on her own, one of his first requests was to see a Broadway show, which she had never imagined he wanted. He also spelled things his partner would not choose to hear. In front of me, he told his mother that a book I'd brought was boring, and she was embarrassed. On another occasion, when he came downstairs while his mother was out, he spelled to his father: "Dad, stop giving me chicken nuggets. I just want to spend time together."

But perhaps his most unexpected request came when he spelled out that he wanted to go to Disney World for his sixteenth birthday, something the family would never have expected, given his sensitivity to crowded and noisy places. They went; he wore noise-cancelling headphones, and he had a blast. "I tolerated it because I wanted to be there," he told me, and made fun of how his father threw up on rides.

A cueing account says the words come from his mother's expectations. However, these messages went against what his family expected, and they changed how the family lives with him. This is exactly what we should be looking for when we ask whether a speller is the author of their words: requests, opinions, and jokes that the partner did not anticipate and would not have chosen. The Hans model has no way to produce them.

Comparing a person to a horse responding to signals is not a neutral choice. It fits an old and outdated assumption: that people who don't speak don't understand. For decades, nonspeaking autistic people were labeled profoundly intellectually disabled, often without any assessment that accommodated their motor differences. The young man I visited spent his early school years in a program built around life skills and weather charts, and he calls his current high school classroom what it is: segregated. When a speller's words are dismissed with a one-line reference to Clever Hans, the speller pays the price: in which school they attend, whether their requests are taken seriously, and whether anyone asks for their opinion at all.

And, if you are still not convinced after reading this, perhaps hearing from the nonspeakers themselves will help. Here’s what they have been expressing about the effects of spelling on their lives:

"It was a game changer for me. It provided me with freedom I dreamed about for 15 years. Now, instead of being an observer, I am an active participant."

"Learning to spell changed my life trajectory. Before, I was treated like a toddler, and my world collapsed in on me… doctors, experts, teachers got it all wrong.… So communication is not just a basic need but a human right."

1. Jaswal, V. K., Wayne, A., & Golino, H. (2020). Eye-tracking reveals agency in assisted autistic communication. Scientific Reports, 10, 7882.

2. Jaswal, V. K., Lampi, A. J., & Stockwell, K. M. (2024). Literacy in nonspeaking autistic people. Autism, 28(10), 2503–2514.

3. Alabood, L., Dow, T., Feeley, K. B., Jaswal, V. K., & Krishnamurthy, D. (2024). From letterboards to holograms: Advancing assistive technology for nonspeaking autistic individuals with the HoloBoard. In Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24). ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642626

#4772. The 24 Best Pieces of Hiking Gear, According to Outdoor Editors

Must-pack picks for day hikes, expedition treks, and everything in between.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE BEST HIKING season is in full swing (fall, and we’ll die on that hill). And winter hiking isn’t that far ahead. So, it’s high time to get your go-to trail gear dialed in. Check your backpack for rips, reseal your tent seams, and make sure there’s enough tread on your favorite hiking boots (or shoes).

If anything needs replacing or upgrading, we’ve put together a guide to the best hiking gear, according to continual testing by our team of outdoor editors and experts. From UPF clothing and waterproof shoes to camp stoves and portable power packs, here’s everything we always pack when hitting the trail, whether for a day hike or even looking to be out there for a few days. And for cooler treks, there’s always some cold weather hiking gear made specific for the task.

As an outdoors writer, I’ve spent countless weeks outside each year for decades. During that time, I've put the most popular hiking gear to the test in places like Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of New Hampshire, the vast deserts of Big Bend National Park, Antarctica, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on his top picks, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, usefulness, weight, durability, materials, functionality, and more.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or need the perfect stove for a full-fledged expedition, we've got you covered with the best hiking gear.

The latest version of the Adidas Terrex Freehiker blends understated street-friendly style with serious trail-ready chops. The low-key aesthetic (especially in core black) plays well with just about any casual outfit, making it a great travel-friendly shoe when you want to pack just one. But, with a Continental rubber outsole and liberal use of Gore-Tex, it’s ready for whatever off-pavement adventures you’re cooking up.

Osprey’s Kestrel 45 is the perfect “all things for all hikers” pack, especially for those looking to buy just one bag. The 45-liter capacity is well-sized for day hikes and overnighters. It features a classic rucksack silhouette, but with all the best features of a modern pack, including comfortable straps and a hip belt, plus a well-ventilated back panel. Storage (pockets, loops, and lash points) is well thought out, and it’s hydration reservoir compatible to boot.

Mammut’s deceptively simple Runbold IV hiking pants are among the best we’ve ever worn. The lightweight, four-way stretch fabric and adjustable waistband are crazy comfortable and allow you to move freely on the trail. Four zippered pockets offer just enough storage for your essentials, and all keep everything close to the body thanks to a more streamlined, athletic fit than most.

It’s not quite a hiking boot, a hiking shoe, or a trail runner—it’s somehow neither and all three in one. The lightweight construction and stiff upper support fast-moving day hikes over challenging terrain. A rock-solid blend of technical materials—namely Gore-Tex Invisible Fit, Vibram Megagrip, and ballistic mesh—makes for our favorite hiking footwear of the year. It’s durable, comfortable, sticks to anything, and is completely waterproof too.

At a minimum, a smartphone and satellite messenger are required packing for most hikers these days, so it’s always good to carry backup power for both. Nestout’s 10000mAh Power Bank is compact, relatively lightweight, and waterproof, making this middle-of-the-pack model the perfect solution for most hikers. Every model in the lineup provides USB-C and/or USB-A ports for keeping your most essential gadgets humming in the backcountry.

Hardcore hikers could argue the virtues of Merino versus synthetic until the sun goes supernova. For us, a blended construction of both is best. Smartwool’s new Active Mesh Short Sleeve T takes a mostly Merino wool design and adds just the right amount of Lyocell and polyester. The result is a near-perfect hiking shirt that’s lightweight, breathable, quick wicking, and odor-resistant.

We’ll take a collapsible water bottle over a traditional Nalgene any day of the week. This 1-liter model is lightweight, inexpensive, and collapses down very small when empty. Plus, the capacity and built-in filter make this a no-brainer for using as your main water bottle or as a backup. With even a remotely drinkable water source along your route, you’re guaranteed clean, potable hydration almost indefinitely.

The right insect repellent is key for spraying on both yourself and your gear. For the latter, we treat all of our outerwear (plus boots and socks) with this purpose-built solution from Sawyer. The permethrin-based product is safe for most fabrics and creates a durable, effective layer of skin-safe protection that fends off ticks, mosquitoes, and other bitey bugs while lasting over a month, even when machine-washed.

UPF hoodies suffer from a sea of sameness. That’s why the Path Projects Wadi 2.0 stands out: It feels and performs differently. The difference being the Toray Fieldsensor Byokan fabric that Path Projects uses. It’s a lightweight material that’s just as durable while also wicking moisture incredibly well. A snap on the hood provides even better neck coverage (and keeps the hood on when moving quickly), and welded sleeve cuffs help your sleeves go over your hands or be pushed up.

True to its namesake, Darn Tough’s socks offer bulletproof durability that I haven’t found in any other sock brand. Their Hike Micro Crew is my go-to for every hike with seamless toe construction and a just-right stretch and cushioning that’s just as comfortable at mile 10 or 100. It’s designed with a “performance fit” that stays put without slipping or bunching, which translates to blissful blister-free hiking. It’s pricey compared to other brands, but I’ve had several pairs for years and they still look good as new. Plus, DT backs all of their products with an unconditional lifetime guarantee.

Even for hikers not regularly trekking out after dark, packing a headlamp just in case is wise. This basic model from Black Diamond is simple, easy to use, and budget-friendly. The compact, low-profile design practically disappears in any backpack, and it can run off of two different types of battery (either standard AAAs or BD’s own rechargeable 1500 lithium-ion cell).

Nothing beats a zip-up fleece hoodie as an extra layer for maximum “toss in the backpack” versatility, and Marmot’s PrimaLoft Evolve Aerothermal Hoody has been my go-to for months now. The inside is as soft as a teddy bear, while the 100 percent recycled ripstop polyester shell helps block some wind and light rain. As the name implies, it’s bolstered with a good dose of PrimaLoft Evolve, making it ideal as an insulating layer in cold weather and a standalone outer layer the rest of the year. At just 10 ounces, it’s incredibly lightweight and packs down small, too, meaning it’s perfect as a “just in case” layer.

Your smartphone might be the most expensive piece of gear in your hiking loadout, so why not protect it on the trail? OtterBox’s Sole Series Pack provides rugged protection via a rubberized shell and raised edges to shield your screen—all with a dash of modern style. A clever elastic rope on the back offers extra storage space for small essentials like lip balm or your driver’s license.

You can’t rely on your smartphone in the backcountry. For couples or groups hiking together, dedicated off-grid-ready communication is essential. Rocky Talkie’s Mountain Radio is ridiculously small and clips to a backpack so it stays out of the way until you need it. It’s great for regular check-ins or keeping in contact if you’re ever separated from the group, especially in cell service dead zones. Plus, the four-day battery life is ideal for longer treks.

Trekking poles are a godsend over difficult terrain. For those times when you need to prioritize featherweight, travel-friendly design over hardcore durability and heavy-duty usability, Helinox’s Passport TL115 are superb. They collapse to a pack-friendly 14 inches when not in use, but adjust to accommodate a wide variety of hikers once unfurled to their max length of 45.5 inches. With EVA foam grips, DAC aluminum alloy shafts, and a lightweight design (just 11.5 ounces for the pair), these are the perfect balance for most hikers’ needs.

Read More: Do I Need to Use Trekking Poles?

When even a daypack is a little too much, a sling is just the trick. REI’s Trailmade Hydration Sling is purpose-built for carrying just enough water and your smallest essentials for a few hours on the trail. I love that it includes a HydraPak water bottle (which makes the already reasonable price feel like a steal), but is also hydration reservoir compatible. The interior is roomy enough for up to 4.5 liters’ worth of gear (think car keys, bug spray, trail maps, and the like), and a stretchy pocket on the padded shoulder strap is the perfect place to stash your smartphone.

Packing a camp chair for a day hike or even longer backcountry excursions might seem an unnecessary luxury. But don’t knock it till you’ve tried it. Crazy Creek’s ultra-portable Hex 2.0 folds and rolls for easy transport, but sets up in seconds at camp or vistas to provide the perfect place to pseudo-lounge after a long day on the trail.

The new PreCip Evo Pro is something of a unicorn in waterproof shells. It’s lightweight, packable, and 100 percent seam-taped for maximum waterproofing—heavier duty than most featherweight “just in case” rain jackets, but lighter and more packable than the sort of hardcore shell you’d pack for a week in the PNW backcountry. Translation: It’s the perfect level of protection against rain for most hikers. Plus, it’s reasonably priced to boot.

Peak Design’s entire line of cleverly designed backpacks is endlessly versatile. The entry-level 18-liter version of the brand’s fan-favorite Outdoor Backpack is perfectly suited for fast-moving, light-packing summit assaults and quick day hikes. The design transitions seamlessly from the office (or airport or train station) to the trail with a rugged-enough construction and streamlined aesthetic that provides everything you need and nothing you don’t in a hybrid daypack.

First and foremost, you might not need any gear other than hiking shoes (or boots) and the clothes on your back. Hiking can be as simple as a 20-minute walk on a path to a multiweek expedition through the wilderness. Hiking more than 30 minutes? You probably want to figure out some sort of hydration at the least. The shorter the hike, the less gear (in theory) you should be toting with you.

Depending on how deep in the wilderness you’re going (or not going) will determine what sort of gear you might need. Even if it’s only a hike for a few hours, if you’re going into wilderness it takes a different mindset for preparedness (and gear) than it does walking on a dirt path in a park in town. The more remote your hike, the more gear you will probably end up needing.

Weather is a big factor when going on a hike. In cooler climates (or when going up in altitude) you’ll need to factor in layers for warmth. In warmer climates, water will be even more important and lighter layers that can shed moisture and protect you from the sun are key. The conditions of the trail (wet, muddy, rocky, dry, etc.) also determine your footwear choice.

The great thing about hiking is you don’t need any experience to start. The most veteran hikers can share the same trails with first-timers, and everyone in between. But knowing what you’re capable of and comfortable with is important. Hiking with a friend is always recommended, but if hiking solo, make sure you inform someone of your location and timing.

Mike Richard has traveled the world since 2008. He's kayaked in Antarctica, tracked endangered African wild dogs in South Africa, and survived a near-miss great white shark attack in Mexico. His travel advice has appeared on the websites for Forbes, Travel + Leisure, CNET, and National Geographic. He loves the great outdoors and good bourbon, and (usually) calls Tulsa, Oklahoma home. Mike also enjoys speaking in the third person.

Ryan Brower is the Senior Gear and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he tests the best products in outdoor gear, tech, running shoes, and more. He has written about the outdoors for nearly two decades and was previously the Managing Editor, Content Performance at Gear Patrol. He holds a B.A. in Sport Management and is a Certified Beer Server, having previously covered the craft beer industry. Ryan currently lives on the water in New Jersey with his wife and their dog.

#4771. Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier. Undoubtedly, some uses will prove beneficial, and others harmful. Evaluating the effect of different forms of AI engagement on human flourishing will thus be critical, and we believe our flourishing measure provides a helpful framework by which to do so. The effects of AI on flourishing may also differ across domains of flourishing.

There may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security. It is not guaranteed to do so, and indeed, as per Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity), much of what AI does or does not achieve will depend upon whether the human person and human dignity are made central in the use and diffusion of AI. However, if employed well and equitably, the potential for AI to advance these aspects of human well-being may be substantial.

The effects, however, of AI technologies on more humanistic aspects of well-being, such as meaning, character, or relationships, seem more ambiguous. Rich, developed countries already seem to be struggling with these more humanistic aspects of well-being, possibly in part due to technology. Will AI help or hinder our sense of meaning, our character, our relationships? As always, so much depends on how we use it.

AI technologies with various relational elements have effectively been used for purposes ranging from helping autistic children develop social skills to building the capacity of university students for civil discourse. While such uses arguably always ought to point back to real relationships, these systems may indeed have the potential to truly enhance human relationships.

However, there is another class of chatbots that aims not at enhancing human relationships, but at replacing them. These are chatbots whose principal aim and purpose is friendship and romance. In a recent article, we have argued that such friendship and romance chatbots have no place in a flourishing life. This may seem like an extreme position. After all, what harm is there in having loneliness somewhat relieved if one’s friends or family are proving disappointing?

The problem is that the temporary alleviation of loneliness is not a solution to loneliness. Loneliness, as painful as it can be, is experienced precisely to try to direct our attention, and our longings, towards deeper human connection. That can take a lot of work and time, and may not be fully within our grasp. But that thirst for human connection has a fundamental role in our life, in guiding us towards others.

When AI chatbots have, as their goal, not helping us with human relationships, but replacing them, they will do damage—damage to ourselves, damage to those we might have interacted with, and damage to the social fabric of society. If they satisfy our loneliness, they do so without another person. A chatbot that always seems to understand, that never has needs of its own, that treats neglect with a delight to see us, ultimately makes us weaker in our capacity for real human relationships. We come to have unrealistic expectations of what to hope for in real human relationships. We lose the capacity to grow through the very difficulties and frictions that real human relationships entail. We come to focus on ourselves rather than on providing for the needs of others. Indeed, with AI friendship and romance, there is no one on the other side to whose life we have contributed.

While AI may have some capacity to enhance our relationships (pointing us towards helpful books or resources for particular problems we are wrestling with) and while certain AI chatbot applications may benefit from relational elements (like the training programs above), this is very different from AI chatbots aimed at replacing real relationships. The effects of these are universally and comprehensively detrimental. They harm us, and they harm those around us. Even if we do not feel the negative effects now, or if they seem small, the increasing incapacity for social relationships will over time gradually erode human connection, human community, and the fabric of society. Human relationships are critical for our health and well-being.

In a remarkable turn of events, China, which has been very pro-AI, in July put into place comprehensive legislation restricting the development and marketing of AI tools “that provide emotional care, companionship, support, and other emotional services,” and including a strict ban on tools “excessively pandering to users, inducing emotional reliance or addiction, [or] harming users' relationships with real people.” What does China know that we don’t? They seem to have almost presciently anticipated the likely effects of AI romance and relationships on human society, human relationships, human reproduction, and human community.

There have also recently been some helpful legislative efforts here in the United States, especially for minors. However, we are naïve to think children are the only ones at risk.

While we do think a ban on AI “relationship chatbots” for friendship and romance may be reasonable here (after all, we ban heroin in the United States), some might view such measures as too extreme. Even if so, we nevertheless believe every effort should be made in practice to purge AI friendship and romance from our lives as individuals and as communities. A technology designed to replace human connection is not a neutral technology.

Love—including love of neighbor and even love of enemy—is crucial for the flourishing of our society. In the words of Pope Leo (and others before him), if we are to seek a flourishing society (and to do so in the age of AI), we need to build “a civilization of love.” We need to love and care for one another. We need to be with one another. We need to have the capacity to work through the difficulties and frictions that real relationships entail, and to grow through those struggles. Therein lies our flourishing, for ourselves, for others, and for society. Real human love requires real human people.

#4770. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#4769. Can Testosterone Add Inches to Your Penis?

There are a lot of misconceptions about what testosterone boosters can and can’t do.

Welcome to Testosterone HQ—Men's Health's guide to the exciting, complicated, and revolutionary world of testosterone. For everything you need to know about T, click here.

IF TESTOSTERONE HELPS increase your penis size during puberty, surely taking TRT will help you get a bigger package?

Unfortunately, testosterone works a bit differently once you’re out of your late teens. Here’s what to know about that.

Testosterone, which is produced by your testicles, “plays a key role in the development of characteristics like libido, and growth of the penis and testicles,” says Jamin Brahmbhatt, MD, urologist at Orlando Health. The hormone surges in your body during your tween and teen years to achieve all of these changes (along with deepening of the voice, facial hair, and so on).

The “blast” of testosterone is usually over by your mid- to late teens. Reproductive urologist Paul Turek, MD, says this is because fertility is achieved as the testicles and penis reach adult size.

YOUR PENIS DOES go through some interesting changes as you age, but it doesn’t get bigger.

After testosterone stops surging in your late teens, your sexual development is set for life. Genetics are the main reason your penis grows to its permanent size. “You’re born with the size already determined,” says Dr. Brahmbhatt.

Now testosterone is still being produced in your body when you’re an adult, but it won’t have any further effect on penis size. That biological fact holds true no matter your penis length. One study done by researchers at the University of Utah School of Medicine found that stretched penile length did not have any association with testosterone levels in adult men.

Since the penis consists of spongy tissue, not muscle, there’s no way to build it up on your own. “There are no safe and effective methods for permanently increasing penis size,” says Dr. Brahmbhatt. Penis pumps might help with stronger erections, but they do nothing for overall size.

WHILE TESTOSTERONE HAD an effect on your penis length early on, more won't help now. It might even hurt to take any sketchy T boosters or penis enlargement pills that promise to increase your girth or length. You have no idea whether they’re safe to take or whether they contain harmful ingredients.

A Stanford University study found that the average erect penile length has grown 24 percent worldwide over the past 29 years. The researchers report this is not due to an increase in testosterone levels.

Any change in development in a short amount of time is concerning. One of the authors of the study noted that chemical exposure could be interacting with the hormone makeup of guys—which may also explain lower sperm counts, increases in testicular cancer rates, and lower T levels in men nowadays.

The bottom line is that size doesn’t matter. Your penis health—especially function—does. If you notice any changes in how your penis looks or functions—patchy spots, bumps, curves—definitely don’t ignore them.

And while it’s natural to be curious about how your penis stacks up with other guys, don’t worry. The average penis length is not as big as you think.

#4768. What Is the Strongest Predictor of Divorce?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

How do you avoid getting divorced? By definition, all married couples seek to avoid their marriage falling apart. In wedding ceremonial vows, couples make commitments to each other, which typically include standing by one another’s side in sickness and health, and in times of prosperity and poverty. Marriage is meant to last forever, but it doesn’t always work out as intended. In the United States, 43-46 percent of marriages end in divorce, and that number rises for second or third marriages.1

Divorce is painful and costly. Getting divorced increases one’s risk of experiencing financial strain, drug and alcohol abuse, suicide, poorer health, and interrupted parenting if the couple has children. Despite the high prevalence of divorce and the substantial consequences associated with it, research on why marriages end has largely developed in separate camps: one focused on how couples communicate, another on the personal vulnerabilities each spouse brings into the marriage, and a third on couples’ financial and socioeconomic circumstances. These perspectives had never been directly compared to see which best predicts divorce. Recently, a team of social scientists published an article digging deep into this question.2

The researchers began by recruiting 368 heterosexual newlywed couples from the Los Angeles Project on Newlywed Development who had gotten married within the past 6 months. The study began in 2009-10 and concluded in 2021-22. Over these 12 years, the researchers tracked a variety of metrics from the couples and, of primary interest, which couples got divorced (or were separated). Six key predictor variables were collected, which include:

The vulnerability variables included a score composed of adverse childhood experiences, history of physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use (past 9 months), negative affect (past 30 days), and parents’ marital status. Communication style was assessed by video recording couples’ discussion of a topic or issue in their relationship, which was carefully coded by trained research assistants. Socioeconomic status included typical metrics of education, income, work stability, financial strain, and neighborhood median income. Worth noting is that the sample itself was not necessarily representative of the general U.S. population (lower income than average, largely Hispanic).

By the end of the study, 39 percent of couples were divorced. When all six of the key predictor variables listed above were used together to estimate who got divorced, the evidence pointed to the wife’s vulnerabilities as the only statistically significant predictor of divorce. The wife’s vulnerabilities also predicted a secondary variable measuring how quickly couples ended their marriage. In other words, the more of these vulnerabilities a wife reported (adverse childhood experiences, physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use, frequent negative emotions in the top 25 percent of the sample, or not being raised by married parents), the more likely the couple was to divorce, even after accounting for the other five predictors.

Although speculative, the authors propose a few reasons why this finding occurred. Women tend to handle the lion’s share of domestic and emotional labor in marriages. Women also tend to be more responsive to partners’ needs, have better memory and awareness of relationship events, and notice problems more often. In sum, women with more vulnerabilities may be more likely to reach the decision to exit more often and more quickly.

But are vulnerabilities deterministic of divorce? Not quite. The same study found that communication mattered in an important way. Among couples who communicated especially well, including more warmth, humor, and effective problem solving, and less hostility, the added divorce risk tied to wives’ vulnerabilities largely disappeared. The baggage women carry into a marriage appears real, but strong interpersonal communication seems to buffer against it. The findings point to two places worth investing in: reducing childhood adversity in the first place and offering couples support that works with those personal histories. Knowing where the risk lies doesn’t seal a couple’s fate. It tells them where to put in the work.

1. Amato, P. R. (2010). Research on divorce: Continuing trends and new developments. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(3), 650–666.

2. Smith, M. G., Block, J. M., Bradbury, T. N., & Karney, B. R. (2026). Individual, interpersonal, and socioeconomic predictors of divorce: A 12-year prospective study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000537

#4767. The Spice Rack Brain Hack

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

“He who controls the spice controls the universe.”—Frank Herbert

Spice adds variety to your life. Especially in your microbiome. Studies are increasingly finding that spices can boost the variety of good microbes in your gut. That, in turn, can improve your mood and cognition via the gut-brain axis.

A study by Regina Lamendella and colleagues, published in The Journal of Nutrition, found that blends of herbs and spices—including cinnamon, ginger, cumin, turmeric, rosemary, oregano, basil, and thyme—increased diversity of the microbiome, a measure of health. The best results were with the participants who got the largest dose of spices—about 1 ½ teaspoons a day.

What is so great about spices and herbs? Their main attraction is their high levels of polyphenols—plant chemicals that provide flavor and color. People who eat plenty of polyphenol-rich foods can cut their risk of type 2 diabetes in half and improve their heart health.

Polyphenols suppress enzymes that activate inflammation. They are also antioxidants, further helping to quell inflammation. Cloves have about 15 percent polyphenols by weight, whereas veggies may have only 0.1 percent. Along with their intrinsic anti-inflammatory effects, polyphenols act as prebiotic fiber, feeding your beneficial gut microbes.

The researchers saw an increase in microbes that produce butyrate, an amazing substance that nourishes and heals the cells lining your gut, ensuring that they keep toxins and pathogens out of your bloodstream. Butyrate does more: It can travel to the brain, encouraging the growth of new nerve cells, improving cognition and memory.

The gut-brain axis responds to inflammation by putting you into sickness mode, where you just want to be left alone to lie in bed while your joy evaporates. This behavior is pretty much identical to depression. Depression and anxiety overlap strongly with gut issues, and psychiatrists are increasingly turning to prebiotics and probiotics to augment other treatments. Microbes that can improve your mood are called psychobiotics. While polyphenols boost good bacteria, they also fight harmful bacteria like C. difficile, Salmonella, and E. coli.

It's not exactly news that spices are healthy. Some 2,500 years ago, Hippocrates believed that spices like cinnamon, coriander, and saffron had healing powers. Nutmeg was prescribed for flatulence, and enticingly, ginger was used as an aphrodisiac. The Kama Sutra recommends cardamom, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves for a good time. Spices were, and still are, sexy.

Spices were also expensive. In 410 AD, the Visigoths sacked Rome and held it hostage for a ransom of 5,000 pounds of gold and 3,000 pounds of pepper. At the time, spices were as good as gold. In those days, traders conspired to restrict the supply of spices, ensuring high prices. Their trade routes were kept secret, and excess crops were burned. It was a cutthroat business, but smuggled seeds soon cropped up in tropical farms around the world. Today, supply chains are efficient, and spices are far cheaper, so there’s little to stop you from trying some.

Don't be afraid to play with combinations of spices to create your own custom spice blend. Use it as a rub on fish or meat before cooking or sprinkle some spice on food after it’s cooked. Pro tip: Buy spices whole and grind them just before using to get the maximum joy. Spices have a lot of volatile oils that evaporate over time and deplete the magnificent aromas.

If you have GERD or IBS, start slowly. Spices activate microbes, which can create gas if you overdo it. But over time, your microbes will adjust.

For everyone else, spices are awesome. They may not help you control the universe, but they taste great, and they can improve your mood. Once you get started, you’ll realize that life is too short to be stuck with bland food. Kick it up a notch.

Khine, Wei Wei Thwe, Sumanto Haldar, Shou De Loi, and Yuan-Kun Lee. “A Single Serving of Mixed Spices Alters Gut Microflora Composition: A Dose–Response Randomised Trial.” Scientific Reports 11, no. 1 (2021): 11264. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-90453-7.

#4766. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4765. What If 'I Know' Is Our Biggest Limitation?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Mentally and physically, I was about as flexible as a broomstick. But I had promised myself that when I arrived in Seattle, I would try things that would get me out of my comfort zone—like yoga.

I was a physician with fairly rigid ideas about what made sense and what didn’t fit my worldview. I was also in the habit of always being two steps ahead, planning what came next. Yoga had other ideas. Standing on one leg left no room to plan whether the union of body, mind, and spirit made sense. All I could do was stay in the present moment and focus on one simple task: keeping my body from falling over.

Had I insisted on what I thought I already knew, I could easily have decided yoga wasn’t for me. Instead, I got curious. That curiosity led me to discover the enormous benefits of meditation, helped me make new friendships, deepened my spiritual connection, inspired me to change my career, and led me to meet my wife Danielle at a yoga retreat. I couldn’t have predicted any of it. Looking back, I simply let myself wonder and wander into the unknown.

We begin life curious. Babies reach for things just beyond their grasp, and children ask endless questions about how things work and why people behave the way they do. But as we grow older, we accumulate knowledge, experiences, and beliefs that help us navigate the world. And the more familiar things become, the less likely we are to question them. We start confusing what we know with what we believe, and what we believe with what is actually true.

We form fixed ideas about other people, about how life works, and especially about ourselves. Without realizing it, we turn our assumptions into invisible boundaries. Eventually, our need for certainty can become a surprisingly restrictive force in our lives.

We can travel to 50 countries, try 20 different hobbies, and still be rigid in our thinking. How often do you dismiss something before you give yourself a chance to explore it? You might avoid a new hobby because you’re convinced you won’t be good at it. You decide someone doesn’t like you based on how they looked at you or something they said. Or you accept your inner critic’s verdict that you are not good enough, that you cannot change, or that certain things aren’t possible for you. But are these conclusions facts, or are they interpretations you have never questioned? Genuine curiosity means being willing to question what we believe we already know, particularly about other people.

I recently heard a wonderful story about a woman called Grace, in her late 80s, who, much to her children’s surprise, decided to volunteer at a homeless shelter. She had held rather rigid opinions about people whose backgrounds and circumstances were very different from her own, and everyone expected her to give up after a few days.

Instead, Grace found her role. When new residents arrive, she guides them around, helping them pick up sheets, towels, and food, and walks with them for about an hour. Along the way, they tell her all about their lives. Then she says, “Honey, I love you,” and gives them a hug.

Today, the residents love her. And they are all coming to her birthday party.

Grace had walked in seeing people through the lens of stereotypes. By listening, she discovered their shared humanity and qualities that inspired her: resilience, tenacity, and kindness, even from people who had experienced very little kindness themselves. She told her daughter, “I thought I had something to offer the residents, but it turns out what they give me is so much more profound.”

But to become genuinely curious, we also need the humility to recognize that there is more we don't know than we know. The moment we accept "I know" as the final answer, we close ourselves off to other possibilities. Intellectual humility means being willing to question our own beliefs, acknowledge that we might be wrong, and consider perspectives that differ from our own (Porter et al., 2022).

This openness can also transform how we relate to others. Studies have found that curious people tend to respond less aggressively, even when provoked, and that asking follow-up questions and showing genuine interest makes us more likable to others (Kashdan et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2017). Similarly, a meta-analysis of 515 studies found that getting to know people from different social groups can help reduce prejudice and challenge stereotypes (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006).

Grace's experience at the shelter illustrates this beautifully. By spending time with people she might otherwise have judged from a distance, listening to their stories, and becoming genuinely interested in their lives, she discovered not only unexpected friendships but also qualities she deeply admired.

The next time you catch yourself judging others or yourself, feeling defensive, or becoming convinced that something cannot change, pause and ask:

Perhaps the greatest limitation in our lives isn’t what we don’t know, but what we believe we already know. Curiosity asks us to make peace with how much we don’t know, to let go of the need to have all the answers, and to be willing to say, “I might be wrong” or, simply, “I wonder what would happen if…”

That willingness took me from a yoga mat to a life I never could have planned.

#4764. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.
