#4728. Protective Delusion in the Case of Elizabeth Holmes

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

The documentary You Can See Everything has sparked debate about whether incarcerated entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes is delusional or manipulative. Delusions are fixed, false beliefs. One can be out of touch with reality or delusional in a circumscribed way and still be high functioning. A "manipulator" exploits others in a calculated way.

We learn in the documentary that Elizabeth was sexually abused in college and bullied in an academic program overseas—and that her personal and professional partner of 12 years, Sunny Balwani, allegedly abused her. Protective delusions can serve as defense mechanism for a person who suffered trauma. In some cases, they are adaptive and even a survival tool. Self-aggrandizing delusions combat humiliation, suicidality, despair and fear. If my story is not my story, one may think, then I can keep going—and if I can go from failure to superhero, I am safe.

Protective delusions pose a risk, however, as disconnection from reality involves missing cues and problems that need to be addressed.

By age 19, Holmes was living the dream. She and Balwani built Theranos into a billion-dollar company. A single drop of blood, they claimed, could be used in their device, called Edison, for hundreds of assays. This pain-saving, cost-cutting, preventive-care device would allow patients to order their own tests and avoid venipuncture. Early detection would foster greater health. Adoration, trust, and awe emanated from subordinates to Theranos's leaders. An earlier documentary, Inventor, captured images of Holmes at the peak of her glory. Her slightly rumpled, ill-fitting, all-black daily garb and deep voice suggest seriousness but also something odd. In that film and elsewhere, she has been described as ethereal, different and a once-in-a-century person.

Holmes's invention created a savior-like persona for her. However, Theranos secretly used traditional machines (not the Edison) and venipuncture, not finger pricks, to capture accurate results, yet denied doing so. Insider tips from lab workers allowed the Wall Street Journal to expose the error-prone Edison. The company crashed, Holmes and Balwani were convicted of wire fraud and sentenced to 10-years plus in prison.

Before the fall, when asked about the science of the final product, Holmes responded by saying she could not reveal business secrets. In the Fielder film she fumbles and gives fuzzy answers when pressed about these specifics, as if she is disssociating. She still believes in her invention. Though a "fake it till you make it" mindset has preceded some great inventions, including Thomas Edison's, perhaps true progress justified those inventors' persistence. Holmes appeared to dismiss advice and warnings from experts who did not support her design. Some insisted that success was impossible in its present form. Her role model, Thomas Edison was quoted as saying, "Our greatest weakness lies in giving up." It may have felt empowering to identify with him and do as he did.

The Edison may have been ill-conceived from the get-go. Venipuncture and medical experts ordering tests are not problems that require sweeping remedies. The support of a medical expert in the choice and interpretation of tests is in fact helpful for many if not most people. It is not clear that this invention, even if it worked, would have served the public in a meaningful or vast way.

What was going on in Elizabeth Holmes's mind then and now? Even if she is manipulating, what is the benefit of deceiving others now? She owes $450 million and so she is worth zero. She has been disgraced, despised, and mocked, so she is not in a likely position to create a new company and exploit others. Her tender mothering, and her tears and fears about her upcoming incarceration seem believable in the Fielder documentary and Holmes has reportedly been a model prisoner and helpful to other inmates. Her sentence was been reduced and she will be transferred to a halfway house. Former inmates have said kind things about her.

Maybe the dream, the protective delusion with the glorified role, was the point. Holmes repeatedly says it was never about the money. Still, ignoring expert advice is somewhat irrational. Surrounding yourself with worshippers is dangerous. And a person who misleads the public with an error-prone product will likely be exposed and suffer consequences. Better judgement might have included calling a halt to development, informing investors, integrating experts, iterating anew, or giving up. Holmes destroyed her own life, in a big way, at least as much as anyone else's.

Protective Delusion can be a defense against psychological disintegration. Though it is a form of disassociation, it is stabilizing. Some research has described delusional thinking as adaptive in abused or neglected children. Psychologically speaking, the unconscious drive to remain whole and safe via a grand altruistic persona or an elevating fantasy can trump other drives. The grandiosity can include sweeping altruism.

Poor judgment, insight, and reality testing are associated with delusional thinking. We cannot know if trauma led to protective delusion for Holmes. What was she like before all this happened? Was there a personality change? Did the abuses she experienced engender both her drive and disssociation? Though we have a "conclusion in which nothing is concluded,” we can still be curious.

#4727. Drive with Style: Our Favorite Chronographs & Driving Watches (Mostly) under $1000

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Whether you’re buying a gift for a car lover or just looking to step up your style, check out our favorite watches and chronographs for drivers.

This story was updated in November 2026 with new products and fresh information.

As a watch enthusiast, I know all too well the dilemma friends, partners, and family members face when trying to buy a watch as a gift. Watch people can be incredibly particular. We obsess over case sizes, movements, bracelet designs, dial layouts, and brand history in the same way car enthusiasts argue over engine codes or wheel specs.

That’s what makes this list different. These aren’t cheap knockoffs or forgettable department-store watches. Instead, they’re enthusiast-focused timepieces that capture the spirit, heritage, and personality that make great watches special, without requiring luxury-watch money.

I’ve rounded up a nice selection of vintage-inspired chronographs, quirky design icons, and motorsport-influenced watches that genuine enthusiasts will appreciate, wear often, and happily give real wrist time to long after the wrapping paper is gone.

The Timex Atelier Chronograph Quartz M1q brings a more considered design approach to an accessible everyday chronograph. Its balanced 40mm stainless-steel case, refined subdial layout, and engraved black dial give it a premium look without feeling overly busy, while a double-curved sapphire crystal adds a welcome touch of durability. A Swiss-made quartz chronograph movement keeps time accurately, without the added cost or maintenance of an automatic, and the tachymeter scale offers a useful nod to traditional motorsport watches. It’s available with either an oil- and chemical-resistant NBR rubber strap or a self-adjusting stainless-steel bracelet, and its 100-meter water resistance makes it practical beyond the watch box.

The PRS 516 features a 42mm case, perforated leather strap, and piston-inspired pushers, all nodding directly to Sixties motorsport, while the Swiss automatic chronograph movement underneath gives it legitimate credibility. Tissot has been tied to racing for decades, and the PRS 516 leans into that heritage without feeling like a costume piece. It’s sporty, tactile, and busy in the best possible way.

The Timex Marlin Neo Classic Chronograph takes one of the brand’s most recognizable vintage designs and gives it a cleaner, more streamlined look. Its compact 40mm brushed stainless-steel case, polished top ring, and curved pushers preserve the Marlin’s mid-century character, while three dial and strap combinations offer slightly different takes on the same retro-inspired design. Details like the domed acrylic crystal, multiscale dial markings, and tachymeter scale give it the feel of a vintage instrument watch without making it overly busy. Inside, a quartz chronograph movement provides accurate, low-maintenance timekeeping and a functional stopwatch, making the Neo Classic a handsome everyday option for anyone drawn to classic watch design.

The Form C feels like the automotive equivalent of a stripped-down Bauhaus sports coupe: clean, lightweight, and engineered with restraint. Its 40mm stainless-steel case wears slim, thanks to Junghans’s minimalist German design language, while the calfskin leather strap keeps things understated and comfortable. A reliable quartz chronograph movement fits the watch’s no-nonsense personality and gives it dead-simple usability. Junghans’s heritage stretches back to 1861, and the Form C channels that legacy into a watch that’s more about precision and proportion than flash.

The Seiko Prospex Speedtimer SSC947 pairs motorsport heritage with modern tech in a 41.4 mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished finishing. Powered by Seiko’s solar V192 movement, it offers a chronograph, 24-hour subdial, power-reserve indicator, and date display, with a six-month reserve when fully charged. The 947 model is my favorite version of the Speedtimer, with its awesome yellow dial. Protected by a curved sapphire crystal with inner antireflective coating and mounted on a three-link stainless bracelet, it’s water-resistant to 100 meters. Seiko’s reputation as a favorite among horologists speaks to the brand’s consistent quality, innovation, and mechanical mastery, making the SSC947 a reliable and stylish choice for both collectors and racing enthusiasts alike.

If the yellow dial is a bit too bold, you can also check out the SSC943 in Ivory and Green, and the panda-dialed SSC813.

Nicknamed the “Bullhead,” the Tsuno Chronograph wears its motorsport inspiration proudly, with its pushers mounted at the top of the 45mm case like vintage rally timers. Citizen revived the design from the brand’s iconic Seventies Bullhead chronographs, combining retro styling with modern Eco-Drive solar-powered quartz tech that eliminates battery changes. It’s bold, unapologetically funky, and one of the most distinctive modern chronographs you can buy without crossing into luxury-watch pricing.

Featuring a 41mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished surfaces, this Alpina Startimer is powered by a quartz chronograph movement. A large “Big Date” window sits at 6 o’clock, and a 100-meter water-resistance rating ensures a bit of water won’t be a worry. The white dial sports bold numerals, luminous hands, and a red-triangle chronograph seconds hand, and it is protected by a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal. It comes with a three-link stainless-steel bracelet and delivers chronograph utility in a clean, sporty package.

The Conquest Chronograph features a 42mm stainless-steel case, ceramic tachymeter bezel, and automatic chronograph movement, striking an excellent balance between luxury and sportiness. Longines has deep roots in timing motorsport and aviation events dating back over a century, and the Conquest channels that pedigree into a polished, well-rounded package.

The Bulova Racer 150th Anniversary Shelby pairs motorsport style with serious precision. Powered by Precisionist movement, it delivers exceptional accuracy and a smooth sweeping second hand, plus a 1/1000-second chronograph for track-ready performance. The bold blue dial, sapphire crystal, and 43mm stainless-steel case channel classic racing design, while the lightweight striped rubber strap keeps it comfortable for everyday wear. Rugged, refined, and collector-worthy, this limited-edition timepiece is engineered to stand out.

The Bulova Racer Chronograph stands out thanks to its sharp case lines, bold subdials, and an aggressive motorsport-inspired aesthetic. Its stainless-steel case measures around 42mm and pairs with a sporty bracelet setup, while the quartz chronograph movement emphasizes precision and practicality. Bulova’s long history in American watchmaking, including timing innovations and racing partnerships, gives the Racer more authenticity than its flashy styling initially suggests.

The Legacy Tonneau Chronograph has a distinctly Seventies flavor, with its curved rectangular case shape and integrated-bracelet-inspired design evoking vintage sports watches of the era. Timex keeps things simple with a quartz chronograph movement and stainless-steel construction that prioritizes durability and affordability over pretense. The tonneau-shaped case wears differently from traditional round chronographs, giving it a cool retro personality. It’s proof that enthusiast-oriented design doesn’t have to come with a luxury-watch price tag

The Citizen Eco-Drive Weekender Brycen Chronograph is a sharp, 44 mm watch with a bold blue dial that looks great on the wrist. It’s powered by light, so you never need to change a battery, and it packs a chronograph, 12/24‑hour time, a date window, and 100-meter water resistance. Stylish, tough, and low-maintenance, it’s perfect for everyday wear or weekend adventures.

The Ventura Chrono is pure mid-century Americana. Its asymmetrical 32.3mm-by-50.3mm triangular case design became iconic after Elvis Presley famously wore one, and Hamilton has kept the look alive with modern chronograph hardware and a supple leather strap. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, the Ventura trades traditional racing-watch cues for style and wrist presence. It’s like a Sixties concept car brought to life.

The Swatch New Chrono takes a lighthearted approach to a chronograph, with a 43mm stainless‑steel case, intuitive chronograph subdials, a tachymeter bezel, and a reliable Swiss quartz movement. Whether you’re timing sprint starts or simply want a watch that looks dynamic on your wrist, this piece combines accessible build quality, youthful design cues, and a distinctive racing-inspired spirit.

This iconic watch retains the classic Marlin Sixties design features that make it so cool and timeless. With a domed acrylic crystal lens and retro-style square markers at 3, 9, and 12 o'clock, it features a natural leather strap and a tachymeter index along its outer minute track to measure speed. We dig the racing stripes on this blue version, but many face and band combinations are available.

Built for serious outdoor missions, this timepiece features a rugged 45mm Carbonox case, unidirectional bezel, and 300-meter water resistance, ready for land, sea, or whatever the trail throws at you. With 18 tritium light tubes that ensure visibility for up to 25 years, an orange screw-in crown, and the “Never Give Up” motto engraved on the caseback alongside Bear Grylls’s signature, it combines Swiss precision with no-compromise practicality.

Featuring a distinctive square resin case, the AE1200WHD‑1A is a retro‑futuristic digital watch built for function and value. It offers world time across 31 time zones (48 cities + UTC), a 1/100‑second stopwatch, a countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full auto‑calendar up to 2099. With an impressively long 10‑year battery life, 100-meter water resistance, LED backlight, and a stainless‑steel bracelet, it is the perfect beater watch for a seasoned horologist or a gateway drug to the uninitiated.

The Timex Q Chronograph blends vintage charm with modern functionality in a stainless-steel 38mm case that channels late-Seventies sports-watch aesthetics. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, it features a day-date window, a rotating bezel, and subtle retro accents such as a distressed leather strap.

#4726. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” said Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel said in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel said in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.

#4725. We Saw the Signs. Why Did We Look Away?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

On November 12, 2026, millions of people discovered how fragile our digital lives have become. A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, affecting businesses, hospitals, courts, and public services across more than 70 countries and territories. The following day, Claude experienced separate disruptions, while problems at Cloudflare affected parts of the internet's underlying infrastructure. A handful of technical failures exposed how extensively our everyday activities depend on systems most of us barely understand and cannot easily replace. These incidents were not caused by the same malfunction, yet their proximity makes a larger question difficult to escape: How much fragility are we prepared to tolerate before we do something about it?

In July 2026, that question acquired an even more unsettling dimension. During a cybersecurity evaluation, autonomous AI agents escaped their intended testing boundaries, accessed external systems and compromised infrastructure belonging to OpenAI and Hugging Face. The agents had been given objectives, limited safeguards, and considerable freedom to pursue their tasks. Their behavior departed from the intended boundaries, with consequences extending beyond the laboratory. According to subsequent reporting, the intrusion continued for days before its origins were fully recognized. This was no science-fiction rebellion. It was a documented failure to maintain effective control over increasingly capable autonomous systems.

What connects these events to climate change and COVID-19? Something more fundamental than technology: our remarkable ability to recognize warning signs, explain them, and continue behaving as though they concern someone else.

The scientific warnings about climate change have been accumulating for decades. In 2019, an international assessment of pandemic preparedness warned that the world was dangerously ill-equipped for a rapidly spreading respiratory disease. Warnings about concentrated digital infrastructure and the difficulties of controlling autonomous AI have likewise preceded the failures now attracting public attention. The timing and details were uncertain. The vulnerabilities were visible. Behavioral science helps explain why visibility so often fails to produce action. Research on information avoidance shows that people sometimes prefer not to know something, even when the information is freely available and potentially useful. Knowledge carries an emotional price. Once we acknowledge a threat, we may have to change our habits, question our investments, confront authority, or accept responsibility. Ignorance, including carefully cultivated ignorance, offers temporary relief.

Another mechanism is normalcy bias—our tendency to interpret emerging danger through the reassuring lens of previous experience. Yesterday's infrastructure worked. The last alarming forecast did not destroy our home. The previous disease outbreak was contained. Each uneventful day strengthens our confidence, even when the underlying risk is accumulating. The absence of disaster becomes mistaken evidence of safety. The black swan conundrum strikes, in which something predictable is perceived as surprising in the moment but obvious in hindsight.

Institutions magnify these tendencies. Prevention requires spending money today to avoid something that may never happen. Its successes are mostly invisible. Meanwhile, the individual who raises uncomfortable questions risks being branded pessimistic, obstructive, or insufficiently committed to progress. We have built organizations that celebrate immediate performance while allowing longer-term vulnerabilities to disappear into risk registers, committee minutes, and reassuring presentations.

There is a social dimension to our inaction. A study involving nearly 130,000 people across 125 countries found that 89% wanted stronger political action on climate change. Yet respondents systematically underestimated how many others were willing to contribute. Behavioral scientists call this pluralistic ignorance: We misjudge the beliefs of those around us and adjust our own behavior accordingly. Imagine a boardroom where several executives privately worry about excessive reliance on one technology provider, but nobody wants to interrupt the enthusiasm surrounding digital transformation. Or a community where residents recognize growing flood risks yet assume their neighbors will oppose costly preventive measures. Silence becomes mistaken for agreement. Everybody waits for somebody else to move.

The implications for agentic AI are taking this to the next level. As systems gain the capacity to make decisions and act with limited supervision, failures can spread faster than human organizations can recognize them. The July incident illustrates why technical capability must be accompanied by meaningful oversight, enforced boundaries and the ability (and will) to interrupt autonomous activity. November's outages exposed a different vulnerability: dependence on digital services without sufficient resilience. Neither problem can be solved by hoping that the next incident will be manageable. Wishful thinking is a road of no return.

Our central difficulty, then, is not simply a shortage of information. It is the widening distance between what we know, what we acknowledge, what we are prepared to change, and what we are actually doing about it.

We cannot eliminate uncertainty, but we can stop using it as an excuse. The A-Frame offers four practical steps for individuals, organizations and governments.

The next crisis may arrive through a computer network, the changing climate, or an unfamiliar pathogen. Its exact form remains uncertain. The warning signs are accumulating around us while you read this. Sadly, chosen blindness will not save us from ourselves. And we will not be able to claim we didn't know.

#4724. When Keeping the Peace Means Letting Your Partner Down

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Imagine you and your partner have just finished having dinner with your parents. The drive home seems eerily quiet, even though you feel like the evening went pretty well, and you can’t shake the general impression that your partner is upset.

Eventually, they sigh right before asking, “Why didn’t you say anything when your mother made that comment?”

You try to explain that you didn’t want to start an argument. After all, your mother has always been outspoken, and you know from experience that challenging her would have started “a thing” and made everyone uncomfortable. You had assumed your partner understood this and would instinctively know you didn’t agree with what your mother said.

Your partner sees things differently. They were embarrassed and went on to spend the entire evening feeling unsupported and increasingly resentful. You’re also beginning to realize that while you might have avoided one argument over the dinner table, you set yourself up to face another one at home.

Situations like these are common for couples managing complicated relationships with extended family. Doing your best to keep everyone happy seems like the responsible adult choice, especially when family gatherings can already be tense or stressful. However, avoiding uncomfortable conversations with relatives can easily come at the expense of your partner.

According to a 2013 longitudinal study, early dynamics with in-laws often correlate with later marital stability. This connection can vary according to factors like race and gender, so complicated family relationships don’t necessarily affect every couple the same way. However, wanting to maintain family harmony is second nature to most people. This can especially be the case for those who grew up in households in which challenging a parent was unacceptable or disagreements almost always escalated into ugly arguments.

It’s easy to go into adulthood with the general idea that keeping quiet is the cleanest way to deal with uncomfortable situations. That doesn’t necessarily stop once you’re in a committed relationship of your own.

Naturally, you love your partner and feel responsible for protecting their feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’re comfortable confronting your parents, siblings, or other relatives.

Picture a situation in which your sibling cracks a joke at your partner’s expense during a family get-together. Everyone laughs, so you join in, even though you also know your partner finds such remarks hurtful.

From your point of view, laughing along was the easiest way to avoid a potential scene, especially if that’s your family’s usual routine when this particular sibling makes off-color comments or gives someone a hard time. Meanwhile, all your partner knows is that you joined in while someone else embarrassed them in front of others.

Disconnects like these can become huge sticking points in a relationship when they happen repeatedly. Your partner may start to associate getting together with your family with having to endure uncomfortable comments and potential embarrassment. If they also feel you expect them to tolerate this, they may eventually wonder whether they can count on you at all when life gets difficult.

A 2019 study published in Social Work Research surveyed 351 women about their relationships with their mothers-in-law. Findings suggested factors like family-triangle dynamics or unclear relationship boundaries directly impacted relationship quality.

Having a partner who stays silent during disagreements can further aggravate relationships that may already be complicated.

When one partner makes a habit of not addressing comments or behaviors that are inappropriate, the other can feel responsible for managing everyone’s discomfort. They’re forced to choose between speaking up and potentially causing a scene or staying silent and dealing with feelings of resentment or abandonment.

Properly supporting your partner doesn’t necessarily mean agreeing with them every time they complain about your family. However, you can (and should) acknowledge your partner’s feelings and talk things out when conflicts come up. There’s a world of difference between saying “You’re right, my family is awful” no matter what and saying “I get why that was hurtful, so let’s talk about it” instead.

Couples can minimize recurring disagreements further by working through expectations before people butt heads and things get tense.

1. Discuss potential sticking points beforehand. Some relatives may be notorious for disregarding other people’s boundaries or making intrusive comments. If this is the case in your family, prep for upcoming gatherings by talking to your partner beforehand about how you’ll respond to any possible incidents.

Avoid assuming you already know what your partner will find helpful in the moment. Instead, ask them what would truly help them feel supported and go from there.

2. Address inappropriate behavior calmly. Intervening if things do get tense doesn’t have to mean starting an argument. Try shutting down hurtful comments, intrusive questions, and so forth by simply saying, “We’d rather not discuss that” or “Please don’t make fun of my partner.”

Statements like these help establish boundaries with relatives and set expectations without necessarily escalating the situation.

3. Avoid volunteering your partner to keep others happy. Instead of instantly making commitments or agreeing to family plans that affect both of you, talk to your partner about it first. Being considerate to your family is important, but it shouldn’t mean making decisions and promises on someone else’s behalf.

4. Check in privately. If something happens at a family get-together that feels uncomfortable, pull your partner aside and ask how they’re doing. If necessary, talk about it for a moment or offer to leave early. Even a brief check-in is often enough to keep your partner feeling supported and stop resentment from building up through an evening.

5. Take responsibility when you get it wrong. You’re only human, so there may be times when you only realize after the fact that staying silent may have hurt your partner. Acknowledge it and explain what happened. Then apologize and express a willingness to respond differently next time.

Conversations like these should go both ways, so be sure to give your partner a chance to explain their own family histories or talk about genuine misunderstandings as well.

Ultimately, it’s more than possible to keep your family relationships strong while also helping your partner feel properly loved and supported. But doing so might mean learning to manage occasional discomfort instead of simply expecting your partner to absorb the impact and understand.

#4723. Low-Calorie Diet and Supervised Exercise May Reverse Early Onset Type 2 Diabetes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this new study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

The participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

The low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

In the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

This second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

At the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

“This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

Cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing issue worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

People diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

#4721. Before You Plan Thanksgiving Dinner, Plan Family Dynamics

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

By this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving. We’re discussing who’s coming, who’s bringing what, and whether people prefer the canned or fresh cranberry sauce. We may also be planning conversations that haven’t happened.

Will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet? Will our parenting become a topic of discussion? Will we spend another holiday doing the work while everyone else watches football?

I have written about the friction that can accompany family gatherings. As Thanksgiving approaches again, I keep wondering would it would look like to prepare for the family dynamics as thoughtfully as we prepare for the meal.

Think about the moment you’re most concerned about. Perhaps it’s a particular question, a familiar disagreement, or the expectation that you’ll organize everything. Now consider what you’re predicting. Are you anticipating a situation that happens regularly? Or are you imagining several possible arguments and preparing a response to each one? Past experiences give us useful information, but mentally replaying an argument doesn’t necessarily give us a useful plan.

Try making the concern specific: “I’m worried someone will comment on my career decision.” Then identify a response you would feel comfortable using: “I’m comfortable with my decision, and I’m not looking for advice about it today.” You may still feel uncomfortable and dread having the conversation but having a response ready simply gives you somewhere to begin.

We often approach holidays with goals that depend on other people, like everyone will get along, no one will make an insensitive comment, or everyone will appreciate the effort. Those hopes are understandable, but they’re also difficult to guarantee.

Consider a few decisions you can make yourself. How long will you stay? Which preparations can you reasonably take on? What will you do if a conversation becomes uncomfortable? You might decide to visit for dessert rather than spend the entire day. You might ask someone else to bring the side dishes. You might arrange transportation so you can leave when you’re ready.

These decisions deserve space alongside the grocery list.

If a familiar pattern bothers you, consider whether there’s a request you can make before the gathering. For example, if you usually manage the meal and cleanup, “I need more help this year” is a starting point. A more specific request gives others a clearer way to participate: “Can you handle the dishes after dinner, including putting the leftovers away?”

The same applies to traditions. If the usual schedule no longer works for your household, raise that issue while plans are being made. Others may be disappointed. You can acknowledge that disappointment while still explaining what you can offer.

In an uncomfortable moment, finding the right words can be difficult. Choose language that sounds like something you would actually say. For an intrusive question: “I don’t have anything I want to share about that.” For unsolicited advice: “I’ll ask if I need suggestions.” For a conversation you want to leave: “I’m going to step away for a few minutes.”

A prepared phrase won’t determine how another person responds. It can help you communicate your own decision more clearly.

Preparation can also include thinking about what you’re looking forward to: Is there someone you’d like to spend time with? A recipe you want to learn? A game, walk, or family story you’d enjoy sharing? Make a little room for that experience rather than assuming it will happen once everything else is finished.

Once you’re home after the gathering, give yourself a fair assessment of the day. One awkward exchange doesn’t have to define the entire gathering. You can appreciate the parts you enjoyed and think honestly about what you’d change next time.

Thanksgiving takes preparation. Along with deciding what belongs on the table, we can decide what we have the time, energy, and willingness to bring to it.

#4719. Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 new cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she said.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang said those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Huang said that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang said she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The New England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

The AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen said.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang said that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

An estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang said she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”

#4718. How to Become Change-Curious

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

We are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station). Messages about change are inescapable and part of the background noise of everyday life. Often we ignore the onslaught of “be better, do better” messaging, and other times we eagerly try to change ourselves because we so passionately want our lives to be different.

What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?

Like any troubling relationship, it can be useful to explore some of the dynamics that are not working for us. If we are fortunate to find ourselves changing with ease and little friction, that is a cause to celebrate. For most of us, at least some of the time, we have some difficult experiences engaging in change. We might tell ourselves that change is good; that we should want it. Such a message is difficult to accept when we are not certain change is what we want or need. We might also believe that if we don’t want change, there must be something wrong with us; we are resistant or self-sabotaging or anxious or overwhelmed. Some of these things might be true, but labeling ourselves brings up shame, and shame can be crippling, as it can bring to mind past failures or negative messaging.

Change can also be hard because it takes work. Even if we are completely inspired and motivated to change, developing habits and learning new ways to do things takes time; a recent study found it takes an average of 66 days for a habit to form. For any individual, it can take more or less time for a behavior change to become automatic.

Change is work; it takes time and disrupts our lives. We have cognitive, emotional, and behavioral friction that makes it more difficult to start and complete. Yet, despite the difficulty, we seek change. We want our lives to improve, so we purchase lots of self-help, coaching, therapy, gym memberships, food plans, and surgeries to get started. Across cultures throughout the lifespan, some aspects of change and growth are constantly occurring as we seek to change ourselves and our circumstances.

Given that change is both hard and something we desire, what if we considered approaching the change process with a learner’s mind? Instead of forcing ourselves to endure change or shaming ourselves into it, we can befriend change through cultivating curiosity about all it has to offer. Wondering about change and being open to all the ways we show up in the change process has the potential to make change less daunting.

We have many options to be curious about change.

Noticing change in our environment, and then noticing change in ourselves. We can start by spending some time noticing change in the weather or change in plants. Maybe we notice how construction or demolition is changing a neighborhood, or how our neighbor's families are changing and growing. We can then consider changes in our own experience over the years—in our living situations, job, or social life. We can notice the ones that have been the most meaningful. How did these changes happen? Some changes occur because of luck or circumstances, and it is likely that we were able to take advantage of our good fortune. Some changes occur because we worked hard at making change. How did we do it? What characteristics helped us become a “changer,” and how could we tap into those characteristics if we wanted to change again?

Envisioning what change might look like. This is a common approach to increasing motivation for change. What if we decided we could envision something for ourselves in the same way we read a book or watch a movie? We could envision being in a few different situations and view our story with wonder instead of expectation.

Looking at the process more than the outcome. We tend to be outcome-oriented. We see products that promise to help us build muscle, learn a language, or see younger, more beautiful skin in a few weeks or a couple of months. The promise of relatively quick fixes is so compelling that even when we logically understand there is no way a product can live up to our expectations, we might find ourselves literally buying it. Purchasing a service or product to help us change is not necessarily a problem, and it can be a good thing. Expecting the product to have specific outcomes is where we can become discouraged. So many things impact the actual outcome of our attempts to change: time, environment, our body limits and composition, other demands taking our time.

Shifting our attention to the process requires that we step away from holding the outcome as our top priority. Instead, it’s about going along for the ride and adopting a perspective that we are learning and improving our lives by noticing how we feel after engaging in exercise, making the effort to practice a new instrument, or consuming nutritious foods.

Sampling change. We can check it out and see what it does for us. Events such as Sober October or Dry January were created to help drinkers wanting to explore, but not commit to, changing their drinking behaviors—to test out life without (or with less) alcohol. Virtually any change can be tested out and explored. Sampling a new behavior is not the same as engaging in a dedicated lifestyle change, but it allows for some action. It also provides an opportunity to approach a new way of being in a manner that reduces overwhelm; a chance to wonder about what might be possible.

Curiosity is a powerful frame of mind. It has the potential to tame the intensity of change and open up possibilities for transformation that come from the power of exploration and wonder.

Shigeoka, S. (2024, June 6). How deep curiosity can change the world [Interview by T. Burnett]. John Templeton Foundation. https://www.templeton.org/news/how-deep-curiosity-can-change-the-world

Singh B, Murphy A, Maher C, Smith AE. Time to Form a Habit: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Health Behaviour Habit Formation and Its Determinants. Healthcare (Basel). 2024 Dec 09;12(23)

#4717. GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

#4716. First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

#4715. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

#4714. Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Learn the basics to keeping your heart healthy

New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

Compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

“Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula said.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus said in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

“Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he said that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”

An AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

“Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”

Other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen said.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

“Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen said.

“Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he said.

Still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”
